# URI

## module `URI`

### `parse`

```kex
parse(text: String) -> Result<URI, URIError>
```

Parses an RFC 3986 URI reference, which may be relative.

The text must be ASCII, with anything else already percent-encoded; use `URI.fromIRI` for text a person typed. Use `URL.parse` when the input must be a complete URL with a scheme and host.

**Parameters**

  - `text` — an absolute URI or a relative reference

**Returns**: the reference, or what is wrong with it

**Examples**

_Resolving an image link found in a document_

```kex
let reference = URI.parse("../images/logo.svg").try
let absolute = base.resolve(reference).try
```

### `fromIRI`

```kex
fromIRI(text: String) -> Result<URI, URIError>
```

Converts an internationalized address (an IRI) to an ASCII URI.

The host is converted with IDNA, and the rest of the non-ASCII text is percent-encoded as UTF-8. Use it for addresses people type or paste; `parse` rejects non-ASCII text.

**Parameters**

  - `text` — the internationalized address

**Returns**: the converted URI, or why it cannot be converted

**Examples**

```kex
URI.fromIRI("https://münich.example/straße").try.string
# => "https://xn--mnich-kva.example/stra%C3%9Fe"
```

## record `URI`

Parses, builds and resolves URIs and URLs, and encodes query strings and HTML forms.

Parsing follows RFC 3986 strictly and keeps the text as it was written: `string` gives back the exact input. Normalizing is a separate step, done by `normalize` and `equivalent?`.

```kex
using URI

let base = URL.parse("https://example.test/a/").try
let reference = URI.parse("../items?limit=10").try
base.resolve(reference).try.string   # => "https://example.test/items?limit=10"
```

A parsed RFC 3986 URI reference: an absolute URI or a relative one.

Make one with `URI.parse` or `URI.fromIRI`, which check the syntax.

**Fields**

  - `source` : [String](string.md#make-string)

Implements [`Showable`](kex.md#trait-showable), [`Inspectable`](kex.md#trait-inspectable).

### Functions

#### `string`

```kex
string -> String
```

Returns the URI exactly as it was parsed.

**Returns**: the URI text

#### `normalize`

```kex
normalize -> URI
```

Returns the URI in RFC 3986 normal form.

The scheme and host are lowercased, needless percent escapes are decoded, and `.` and `..` path segments are resolved. Parsing never does this by itself, because signatures, cache keys and logs may depend on the exact text.

**Returns**: the normalized URI

**Examples**

```kex
URI.parse("HTTP://example.com/%7Eada").try.normalize.string
# => "http://example.com/~ada"
```

#### `equivalent?`

```kex
equivalent?(other: URI) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the two URIs are the same after normalizing.

`==` compares the text as written.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the URI to compare

**Returns**: `true` when both normalize to the same URI

**Examples**

_Spotting the same link spelled two ways_

```kex
URI.parse("HTTP://example.com/%7Eada").try
  .equivalent?(URI.parse("http://example.com/~ada").try)
# => true
```

#### `resolve`

```kex
resolve(reference: URI) -> Result<URI, URIError>
```

Resolves `reference` against this URI, as a browser resolves a link against the page it is on.

**Parameters**

  - `reference` — the relative or absolute reference

**Returns**: the resolved URI, or a `NotAbsolute` error when this URI is relative and cannot serve as a base

**Examples**

_Following a relative link_

```kex
let base = URI.parse("https://example.com/docs/start").try
base.resolve(URI.parse("../api").try).try.string
# => "https://example.com/api"
```

#### `scheme`

```kex
scheme -> String?
```

Returns the scheme in lowercase, or `None` for a relative reference.

**Returns**: the scheme, or `None`

#### `host`

```kex
host -> Host?
```

Returns the host, or `None` when the URI has none.

**Returns**: the host, or `None`

#### `query`

```kex
query -> Query?
```

Returns the query, or `None` when the URI has no `?`.

A URI ending in a bare `?` has a query with no entries, which is not the same as `None`.

**Returns**: the query, or `None`

#### `showValue` (from Showable)

```kex
showValue -> String
```

Renders the URI with any password in it replaced by `***`.

#### `inspectValue` (from Inspectable)

```kex
inspectValue(colors: Bool) -> String
```

Renders the URI with any password in it replaced by `***`, as `showValue` does.

### From [`Showable`](kex.md#trait-showable)

  - [`to`](kex.md#showable-to) — 

## record `URL`

An absolute URI with a host, such as an HTTP URL.

Every `URL` has a scheme and a host, so `scheme` and `host` return them directly, where the `URI` versions return optionals. Make one with `URL.parse` or `URL.build`.

**Fields**

  - `source` : [String](string.md#make-string)

Implements [`Showable`](kex.md#trait-showable), [`Inspectable`](kex.md#trait-inspectable).

### Functions

#### `string`

```kex
string -> String
```

Returns the URL exactly as it was parsed.

**Returns**: the URL text

#### `normalize`

```kex
normalize -> URL
```

Returns the URL in RFC 3986 normal form.

**Returns**: the normalized URL

**Examples**

```kex
URL.parse("HTTPS://Example.COM/a/../b").try.normalize.string
# => "https://example.com/b"
```

#### `equivalent?`

```kex
equivalent?(other: URL) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the two URLs are the same after normalizing.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the URL to compare

**Returns**: `true` when both normalize to the same URL

#### `resolve`

```kex
resolve(reference: URI) -> Result<URL, URIError>
```

Resolves `reference` against this URL.

The result must still be a URL, so a reference without a host, such as `mailto:ada@example.com`, is a `MissingAuthority` error.

**Parameters**

  - `reference` — the relative or absolute reference

**Returns**: the resolved URL

**Examples**

_Following an API's pagination link_

```kex
URL.parse("https://api.example.com/v1/items").try
  .resolve(URI.parse("?page=2").try)
  .try.string
# => "https://api.example.com/v1/items?page=2"
```

#### `scheme`

```kex
scheme -> String
```

Returns the scheme in lowercase.

**Returns**: the scheme

#### `host`

```kex
host -> Host
```

Returns the host.

**Returns**: the host

#### `query`

```kex
query -> Query?
```

Returns the query, or `None` when the URL has no `?`.

**Returns**: the query, or `None`

#### `showValue` (from Showable)

```kex
showValue -> String
```

Renders the URL with any password in it replaced by `***`.

#### `inspectValue` (from Inspectable)

```kex
inspectValue(colors: Bool) -> String
```

Renders the URL with any password in it replaced by `***`, as `showValue` does.

### From [`Showable`](kex.md#trait-showable)

  - [`to`](kex.md#showable-to) — 

## record `Host`

A URI's host as written, in `display`, and in lowercase ASCII (IDNA) form, in `ascii`.

**Fields**

  - `display` : [String](string.md#make-string)
  - `ascii` : [String](string.md#make-string)



## record `Query`

The entries of a URI query string, in order.

Order and repeated keys are kept, since APIs rely on them: `tag=kex&tag=beam` has two entries. A value of `None` is a bare key, as in `?debug`; `Just("")` is a key with an empty value, as in `?debug=`.

**Fields**

  - `entries` : [([String](string.md#make-string), [String](string.md#make-string)?)]

### Functions

#### `encode`

```kex
encode -> String
```

Encodes the query by RFC 3986 rules, percent-encoding a +++ in a value.

**Returns**: the encoded query, without a leading `?`

**Examples**

```kex
Query.from([("q", Just("a+b"))]).encode   # => "q=a%2Bb"
```

## record `Form`

The fields of an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, in order.

Forms encode a space as +++. In a `Query`, +++ is a literal plus sign.

**Fields**

  - `entries` : [([String](string.md#make-string), [String](string.md#make-string)?)]

### Functions

#### `encode`

```kex
encode -> String
```

Encodes the form by HTML form rules, which write a space as +++.

**Returns**: the `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body

**Examples**

```kex
Form.from([("query", "hello world")]).encode
# => "query=hello+world"
```

## record `URIError`

The error returned when a URI cannot be parsed, converted or resolved: its `kind`, and a message for a person to read.

**Fields**

  - `kind` : [URIErrorKind](#type-uri-urierrorkind)
  - `message` : [String](string.md#make-string)
  - `position` : [Integer](number.md#make-integer)?



## type `URIErrorKind`

What kind of problem a `URIError` reports.

**Variants**

  - `InvalidSyntax`
  - `InvalidEscape`
  - `InvalidAuthority`
  - `InvalidPort`
  - `NonASCII`
  - `NotAbsolute`
  - `NotHierarchical`
  - `MissingAuthority`
  - `UnsupportedScheme`



## module `URI.URL`

### `parse`

```kex
parse(text: String) -> Result<URL, URIError>
```

Parses an absolute URL with a scheme and host.

A relative reference is a `NotAbsolute` error, and a URI without a host, such as `mailto:ada@example.com`, is `MissingAuthority`.

**Parameters**

  - `text` — the complete URL

**Returns**: the URL, or what is wrong with it

**Examples**

_Checking a webhook URL from the configuration_

```kex
let webhook = URL.parse(ENV.get("WEBHOOK_URL").or("")).try
```

### `build`

```kex
build(scheme: String, host: String, path: [String], query: Query) -> Result<URL, URIError>
```

Builds a URL from a scheme, a host, path segments and a query.

Pass the path segments and query values unencoded. Each segment is encoded on its own, so a `/` inside a value stays part of that segment. The scheme and host are lowercased. The host must be ASCII: an international name has to be given in its `xn--` form.

**Parameters**

  - `scheme` — the URL scheme, such as `https`
  - `host` — the host name, in ASCII
  - `path` — the path segments, unencoded
  - `query` — the query entries, unencoded

**Returns**: the URL, or why it is invalid

**Examples**

_Building an API URL from a name a user supplied_

```kex
URL.build("https", "api.example.com", ["users", "a/b c"],
  Query.from([("include", Just("profile"))])).try.string
# => "https://api.example.com/users/a%2Fb%20c?include=profile"
```

## module `URI.Query`

### `from`

```kex
from(entries: [(String, String?)]) -> Query
from(entries: Map<String, String?>) -> Query
```

Builds a query from a list of entries, keeping their order, repeated keys and bare keys.

A `None` value is encoded as a bare key, and `Just("")` as a key with an equals sign, so `?debug` and `?debug=` stay different.

**Parameters**

  - `entries` — the keys and values, unencoded

**Returns**: the query

**Examples**

_Repeated filters and a bare flag_

```kex
Query.from([
  ("tag", Just("kex")),
  ("tag", Just("beam")),
  ("debug", None)
]).encode
# => "tag=kex&tag=beam&debug"
```

### `parse`

```kex
parse(text: String) -> Result<Query, URIError>
```

Parses a query string, decoding percent escapes.

A +++ stays a plus sign; use `Form.parse` for form bodies, where it means a space.

**Parameters**

  - `text` — the query, without the leading `?`

**Returns**: the entries, or an `InvalidEscape` error

**Examples**

```kex
Query.parse("tag=kex&tag=beam&debug").try.entries
# => [("tag", Just("kex")), ("tag", Just("beam")), ("debug", None)]
```

## module `URI.Form`

### `from`

```kex
from(entries: [(String, String)]) -> Form
from(entries: Map<String, String>) -> Form
```

Builds a form from a list of fields, keeping their order and repeated names.

**Parameters**

  - `entries` — the field names and values, unencoded

**Returns**: the form

**Examples**

_Preparing a login request body_

```kex
Form.from([("email", email), ("password", password)]).encode
```

### `parse`

```kex
parse(text: String) -> Result<Form, URIError>
```

Parses an `application/x-www-form-urlencoded` body, where +++ means a space.

**Parameters**

  - `text` — the encoded body

**Returns**: the fields, or an `InvalidEscape` error

**Examples**

_Reading a search field a browser submitted_

```kex
Form.parse("query=hello+world").try.entries
# => [("query", Just("hello world"))]
```

package: prelude
version: "0.4.0-rc.5-dev"
source: control/retry.kex
title: Control.Retry
entities:
  - { kind: module, name: "Control.Retry" }
---

# Control.Retry

## module `Control.Retry`

Retries an operation that returns an error, with a delay between attempts.

**Examples**

_Retry a request and handle the final result_

```kex
using Control.Retry
using Net.HTTP

let result = Retry.run(attempts: 5) do
  HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/inventory")
end
match result do
  Ok(response) => IO.printLine(response.status.code)
  Error(error) => IO.printLine(error.message)
end
```

_Fixed delays: three waits of 250 milliseconds_

```kex
let schedule = Retry.Schedule {
  attempts: 4, delay: 250.millisecond, backoff: 1.0,
  maximumDelay: 250.millisecond, jitter: 0.0
}
Retry.run(schedule: schedule) do
  Error("not ready")
end
# => Error("not ready"), after four calls and 750 ms of sleep
```

_Exponential delays: 200, 400, 800, 1600 milliseconds_

```kex
let schedule = Retry.Schedule {
  attempts: 5, delay: 200.millisecond, backoff: 2.0,
  maximumDelay: 5.second, jitter: 0.0
}
Retry.run(schedule: schedule) do
  Error("busy")
end
# => Error("busy"), after five calls and three seconds of sleep
```

_Capped delays: 500 ms, 1 s, 2 s, 2 s, 2 s_

```kex
Retry.Schedule {
  attempts: 6, delay: 500.millisecond, backoff: 2.0,
  maximumDelay: 2.second, jitter: 0.0
}
```

_Use one schedule for two requests_

```kex
using Net.HTTP
let schedule = Retry.Schedule { attempts: 5 }
let inventory = Retry.run(schedule: schedule) do
  HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/inventory")
end
let orders = Retry.run(schedule: schedule) do
  HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/orders")
end
# Each request gets up to five attempts, independently.
```

_Set retry options directly_

```kex
Retry.run(attempts: 5, delay: 200.millisecond, jitter: 0.0) do
  Ok("ready")
end
# => Ok("ready")
```

_Limit the time spent sleeping_

```kex
Retry.run(
  attempts: 5, delay: 1.second, backoff: 2.0,
  jitter: 0.0, maximumTotalDelay: Just(2.second)
) do
  Error("busy")
end
# => Error("busy"), two calls and one second of sleep
```

_Test jitter without waiting_

```kex
Retry.run(
  attempts: 2, delay: 4.second, jitter: 0.25,
  sleeper: { |wait| Assert.equal(wait, 3.second) },
  random: { 0.0 }
) do
  Error("temporary")
end
# => Error("temporary"), two calls and one fake sleep
```

_Report progress_

```kex
using Net.HTTP
Retry.run(attempts: 5, onRetry: { |info|
  let progress = "retrying ${info.nextAttempt}/${info.maximumAttempts}"
  IO.printLine("${progress} in ${info.delay.seconds} seconds")
}) do
  HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/inventory")
end
```

_Retry temporary HTTP failures and selected statuses_

```kex
using Net
using Net.HTTP
let schedule = Retry.Schedule { attempts: 5 }
let outcome = Retry.run(schedule: schedule) do
  let result = HTTP.get("https://api.example.com/inventory")
  match result do
    Error(error) => if error.kind == Timeout || error.kind == Connect
      Retry.again(result)
    else
      Retry.done(result)
    end
    Ok(response) => if [429, 502, 503, 504].contains?(response.status.code)
      Retry.again(result)
    else
      Retry.done(result)
    end
  end
end
match outcome do
  Retry.Done(result) => IO.printLine(result)
  Retry.Again(last) => IO.printLine("retry budget exhausted: ${last}")
end
```



## module `Control.Retry.Retry`

Running an operation until it succeeds or a `Schedule` runs out.

`run` calls the block at once. An `Ok` result is returned; an `Error` is retried after a wait, and when the schedule runs out the last error is returned as it is. To choose yourself what to retry, return `again` or `done` from the block.

An HTTP 429 or 503 response is `Ok(response)`, so retrying on a status needs `again`. Only retry a write when repeating it is harmless, for example with an idempotency key. The schedule limits the time spent sleeping, not the time spent in the operation, so give requests their own timeouts.

### `again`

```kex
again(value: X) -> Decision<X>
```

Returns `Again(value)`, asking `run` to try again if the schedule allows.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the result, which `run` returns if the schedule runs out

**Returns**: `Again(value)`

### `done`

```kex
done(value: X) -> Decision<X>
```

Returns `Done(value)`, telling `run` to stop with `value`, whether that is a success or a failure not worth retrying.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the final result

**Returns**: `Done(value)`

### `run` (foul)

```kex
run(operation: Block<X>, schedule: Schedule = …, attempts: Integer = …, delay: Duration = …, backoff: Float = …, maximumDelay: Duration = …, jitter: Float = …, maximumTotalDelay: Duration? = …, sleeper: (Duration -> Void) = …, random: Block<Float> = …, onRetry: (Info<X> -> Void) = …) -> X
```

Calls `operation` until it succeeds, returns `done`, or runs out of attempts or sleep time, and returns its last result.

The first call happens at once, and each later one after a wait. Named timing options override that field of `schedule` for this run only.

When the block returns a `Result`, `Ok` stops and `Error` is retried. When it returns `done(value)` or `again(value)`, it decides itself. Use one of the two forms throughout the block. An error raised inside the block is not caught or retried.

Settings out of range are adjusted, not rejected: attempts below 1 become 1, negative durations zero, a backoff below 1 becomes 1, and jitter and the random samples are clamped to 0..1.

`Done(Error(...))` means the block gave up on an error not worth retrying. `Again(Ok(response))` means a response the block rejected, such as a 503, kept coming until the schedule ran out. `run` knows nothing about HTTP: deciding which statuses to retry and honouring `Retry-After` are up to the block.

`sleeper` and `random` are for tests, and replacing one leaves the other real. A sample of 0 picks the shortest jittered wait, 0.5 the unjittered one, and 1 the longest. With zero jitter `random` is not called. lint:allow parameter-count — named options make each setting independent

**Parameters**

  - `operation` — called once per attempt; returns a `Result` or a `Decision`
  - `schedule` — the settings; defaults to `Schedule {}`
  - `attempts` — total attempts; defaults to the schedule field
  - `delay` — initial wait; defaults to the schedule field
  - `backoff` — delay multiplier; defaults to the schedule field
  - `maximumDelay` — sleep cap; defaults to the schedule field
  - `jitter` — variation fraction; defaults to the schedule field
  - `maximumTotalDelay` — sleep budget; defaults to the field
  - `sleeper` — waits between attempts; defaults to `Task.sleep`
  - `random` — returns a sample in 0..1 for jitter; defaults to a secure random source
  - `onRetry` — called before each wait; defaults to doing nothing

**Returns**: the first `Ok` or `Done`, or the last `Error` or `Again` when the schedule runs out

## record `Schedule`

The attempt limit and the waits `run` uses between attempts.

Every field has a default: three attempts, a first wait of 100 ms that doubles each time up to 5 seconds, and 20% jitter. A schedule only holds settings, so each `run` that uses it starts again from the first attempt.

**Fields**

  - `attempts` : [Integer](../number.md#make-integer) (optional)
  - `delay` : Duration (optional)
  - `backoff` : [Float](../number.md#make-float) (optional)
  - `maximumDelay` : Duration (optional)
  - `jitter` : [Float](../number.md#make-float) (optional)
  - `maximumTotalDelay` : Duration? (optional)



## type `Decision<X>`

A block's decision whether to retry, carrying its result.

From `run`, `Done(value)` means the block chose to stop, and `Again(value)` means it still wanted to retry when the schedule ran out. The value can be anything, including an `Error`.

**Variants**

  - `Again(X)`
  - `Done(X)`



## record `Info<X>`

What `run` passes to `onRetry` just before it waits for the next attempt.

`onRetry` is called only when another attempt will follow, never after a success, a `done`, or the last attempt. The durations count sleep only, not time spent in the operation.

**Fields**

  - `attempt` : [Integer](../number.md#make-integer)
  - `nextAttempt` : [Integer](../number.md#make-integer)
  - `maximumAttempts` : [Integer](../number.md#make-integer)
  - `remainingAttempts` : [Integer](../number.md#make-integer)
  - `delay` : Duration
  - `totalDelay` : Duration
  - `result` : X

package: prelude
version: "0.4.0-rc.5-dev"
source: data/queue.kex
title: Data.Queue
entities:
  - { kind: module, name: "Data" }

# Data.Queue

## module `Data`

A first-in-first-out queue.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Queue`.

```kex
using Data.Queue

let q = Queue.from([1, 2, 3])
q.enqueue(4).items    # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
q.peek                # => Just(1)
```

The queue is two lists. `front` holds the elements next in line, and `back` holds the newest ones in reverse. `enqueue` adds to the head of `back`, and `dequeue` takes the head of `front`, reversing `back` into `front` when `front` runs out. Both run in amortized constant time.

`items` gives the elements as a list, front first.

The same elements can be split between `front` and `back` in different ways: `Queue.from([1, 2])` and `Queue.from([1]).enqueue(2)` differ inside. `==` compares `items`, so it calls them equal. Map keys and record patterns compare the fields themselves, so to them the two queues differ.

Updates return a new queue. `enqueue!` and `dequeue!` rebind the variable instead.



## record `Queue<A>`

A first-in-first-out queue: `front` holds the elements next in line, `back` the newest ones in reverse.

Build one with `Queue.from` or `Queue.empty`.

**Fields**

  - `front` : [A] (optional)
  - `back` : [A] (optional)

Implements [`Enumerable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-enumerable), [`Foldable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable), [`Monoid`](../algebra.md#trait-monoid), [`Showable`](../kex.md#trait-showable), [`Blankable`](../blankable.md#trait-blankable).

### Functions

#### `reduce` (from Enumerable, Foldable)

```kex
reduce(acc: B, f: (B -> A -> B)) -> B
```

Folds the elements from front to back.

The other `Enumerable` and `Foldable` functions are built on this one.

**Parameters**

  - `acc` — the initial accumulator
  - `f` — combines the accumulator with each element

**Returns**: the final accumulator

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2, 3]).reduce(0) { |sum, x| sum + x }   # => 6
```

#### `identity` (from Monoid)

```kex
identity -> Queue<A>
```

Returns the empty queue, the `Monoid` identity.

**Returns**: the empty queue

#### `combine` (from Monoid)

```kex
combine(other: Queue<A>) -> Queue<A>
```

Joins two queues: this one's elements, then `other`'s.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the queue to append

**Returns**: this queue's elements, then `other`'s

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2]).combine(Queue.from([3, 4])).items   # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

#### `items`

```kex
items -> [A]
```

Returns the elements as a list, front first.

**Returns**: the elements, front first

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2]).enqueue(3).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

#### `enqueue`

```kex
enqueue(value: A) -> Queue<A>
```

Returns a new queue with `value` added at the back.

Use `enqueue!` to rebind the receiver variable.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to add

**Returns**: a queue with `value` at the back

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2]).enqueue(3).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

#### `dequeue`

```kex
dequeue -> (A, Queue<A>)?
```

Returns the front element and the queue without it, wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty queue.

When `front` is empty, this reverses `back` into it, which takes time in proportion to its length. Each element is reversed only once, so the cost evens out to constant time per element.

Use `dequeue!` to rebind the receiver variable.

**Returns**: the front element and the rest, or `None`

**Examples**

```kex
match Queue.from([1, 2, 3]).dequeue do
  Just((head, rest)) => (head, rest.items)   # => (1, [2, 3])
  None => (0, [])
end
Queue.empty.dequeue                          # => None
```

#### `peek`

```kex
peek -> A?
```

Returns the front element wrapped in `Just`, or `None` for an empty queue.

**Returns**: the front element, or `None`

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2]).peek   # => Just(1)
Queue.empty.peek          # => None
```

#### `count` (from Foldable)

```kex
count -> Integer
```

Returns the number of elements.

**Returns**: the number of elements

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2, 3]).count   # => 3
```

#### `empty?`

```kex
empty? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the queue has no elements.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty queue

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.empty.empty?         # => true
Queue.from([1]).empty?     # => false
```

#### `==`

```kex
==(other: Queue<A>) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when both queues hold the same elements in the same order, however each splits them between `front` and `back`.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the queue to compare against

**Returns**: `true` when both hold the same elements in the same order

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2]) == Queue.from([1]).enqueue(2)   # => true
```

#### `+`

```kex
+(other: Queue<A>) -> Queue<A>
+(other: [A]) -> Queue<A>
```

Appends the elements of another queue or of a list.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the elements to append

**Returns**: this queue's elements, then `other`'s

**Examples**

```kex
(Queue.from([1, 2]) + [3, 4]).items            # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
(Queue.from([1, 2]) + Queue.from([3])).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

#### `showValue` (from Showable)

```kex
showValue -> String
```

Renders the queue as `Queue(...)`, front to back.

**Returns**: the rendered queue

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2, 3]).showValue   # => "Queue(1, 2, 3)"
```

#### `blank?` (from Blankable)

```kex
blank? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the queue has no elements; the `Blankable` name for `empty?`.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty queue

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.empty.blank?         # => true
Queue.from([1]).blank?     # => false
```

### From [`Enumerable`](../enumerable.md#trait-enumerable)

  - [`map`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-map) — Applies `f` to each item and returns the results as a list.
  - [`mapIndexed`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-mapindexed) — Applies `f` to each item and its 0-based position, and returns the results as a list.
  - [`filter`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-filter) — Returns the items for which `pred` returns `true`.
  - [`into`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-into) — Applies `f`, which returns a list, to each item and concatenates the results.
  - [`collect`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-collect) — Applies `f`, which returns an `Optional`, to each item and returns the present values, unwrapped.

### From [`Foldable`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable)

  - [`each`](../enumerable.md#foldable-each) — Calls `f` with each item, for its side effects.
  - [`eachIndexed`](../enumerable.md#foldable-eachindexed) — Calls `f` with each item and its 0-based position, for its side effects.
  - [`all?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-all?) — Returns `true` when every item satisfies `pred`, and `true` for an empty collection.
  - [`any?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-any?) — Returns `true` when at least one item satisfies `pred`, and `false` for an empty collection.
  - [`none?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-none?) — Returns `true` when no item satisfies `pred`, the opposite of `any?`.
  - [`one?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-one?) — Returns `true` when exactly one item satisfies `pred`.
  - [`find`](../enumerable.md#foldable-find) — Returns the first item satisfying `pred`, or `None` when nothing does.

### From [`Monoid`](../algebra.md#trait-monoid)

  - [`repeat`](../algebra.md#monoid-repeat) — Combines this value with itself `n` times.

### From [`Showable`](../kex.md#trait-showable)

  - [`to`](../kex.md#showable-to) — 

## module `Data.Queue`

Constructors for `Queue`.

### `from`

```kex
from(items: [A]) -> Queue<A>
```

Builds a queue from a list, front first.

**Parameters**

  - `items` — the elements, front first

**Returns**: the queue, ready to `dequeue` in the same order

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.from([1, 2, 3]).peek   # => Just(1)
```

### `empty` (constant)

```kex
empty : Queue<A>
```

Returns the empty queue, which is also the `Monoid` identity.

**Examples**

```kex
Queue.empty.empty?   # => true
```

# Data.Set

## module `Data`

Immutable collections of distinct elements.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Set`, which brings in both kinds of set:

```kex
using Data.Set
```

Membership uses the same structural equality as `==` and map keys, so records and tuples are compared by value. Updates return a new set. The `!` forms (`add!`, `delete!`) rebind the variable they are called on to the new set.

```kex
let tags = Set.from(["kex", "beam", "kex"])
tags.count                     # => 2
tags.contains?("beam")         # => true
tags.add("erlang").items       # => ["beam", "erlang", "kex"]
```

The two kinds differ in how they store their elements:

```kex
Set           kept sorted, so iteration is in ascending order and the
              elements must be +Comparable+.
UnorderedSet  hash-based, so +contains?+ is a map lookup and the elements
              need only support equality. Iteration order is unspecified,
              so don't write a test that depends on it.
```

Use `Set` when you will read the elements back out, and `UnorderedSet` when the set is mostly asked `contains?`.

Two sets are equal when they have the same elements. `items` returns the elements as a list, in no particular order for an `UnorderedSet`.



## record `Set<A>`

A set whose elements are kept sorted and free of duplicates.

Build one with `Set.from`. A `Set { items: ... }` literal neither sorts nor removes duplicates, and every function here assumes both. `items` is the stored list, so reading it costs nothing.

```kex
Set.from([3, 1, 2]).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

**Fields**

  - `items` : [A] (optional)

Implements [`Enumerable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-enumerable), [`Foldable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable), [`Monoid`](../algebra.md#trait-monoid), [`Showable`](../kex.md#trait-showable), [`Blankable`](../blankable.md#trait-blankable).

### Functions

#### `reduce` (from Enumerable, Foldable)

```kex
reduce(acc: B, f: (B -> A -> B)) -> B
```

Folds over the elements in ascending order.

`each`, `find`, `any?` and the rest of `Enumerable` are built on it. `map`, `filter` and `reject` are defined below to return a `Set`; the other `Enumerable` functions that build a collection return a list.

**Parameters**

  - `acc` — the initial accumulator
  - `f` — combines the accumulator with each element

**Returns**: the final accumulator

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).reduce(0) { |sum, x| sum + x }   # => 6
```

#### `identity` (from Monoid)

```kex
identity -> Set<A>
```

Returns the empty set, the `Monoid` identity for union.

**Returns**: the empty set

#### `combine` (from Monoid)

```kex
combine(other: Set<A>) -> Set<A>
```

Returns the union of the two sets. This is the `Monoid` operation.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the set to combine with

**Returns**: every element of either set

**Examples**

_Merging many sets into one_

```kex
[Set.from([1]), Set.from([2]), Set.from([1, 3])]
  .reduce(Set.empty) { |acc, s| acc.combine(s) }
# => Set(1, 2, 3)
```

#### `contains?`

```kex
contains?(value: A) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when `value` is a member.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to look for

**Returns**: `true` when it is present

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).contains?(2)   # => true
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).contains?(9)   # => false
```

_Filtering a list against an allow-list_

```kex
let allowed = Set.from(["get", "post"])
verbs.filter { |v| allowed.contains?(v.lowerCase) }
```

#### `count` (from Foldable)

```kex
count -> Integer
```

Returns the number of elements. Duplicates in the list the set was built from are not counted.

**Returns**: the number of elements

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 1, 2]).count   # => 2
```

_Counting distinct words_

```kex
Set.from(text.split(" ")).count
```

#### `empty?`

```kex
empty? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the set has no elements.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty set

**Examples**

```kex
Set.empty.empty?           # => true
Set.from([1]).empty?       # => false
```

#### `add`

```kex
add(value: A) -> Set<A>
```

Returns a new set with `value` added. Adding an existing member changes nothing.

`add!` rebinds the variable instead.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to add

**Returns**: a set including `value`

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2]).add(3)   # => Set(1, 2, 3)
Set.from([1, 2]).add(2)   # => Set(1, 2)
```

_Accumulating as you go_

```kex
var seen = Set.empty
ids.each { |id| seen.add!(id) }
```

#### `delete`

```kex
delete(value: A) -> Set<A>
```

Returns a new set without `value`. Removing a non-member changes nothing.

`delete!` rebinds the variable instead.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to remove

**Returns**: a set without `value`

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).delete(2)   # => Set(1, 3)
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).delete(9)   # => Set(1, 2, 3)
```

#### `union`

```kex
union(other: Set<A>) -> Set<A>
```

Returns every element of either set.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: the union

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2]).union(Set.from([2, 3]))   # => Set(1, 2, 3)
```

_Collecting every tag used across posts_

```kex
posts.reduce(Set.empty) { |all, p| all.union(Set.from(p.tags)) }
```

#### `intersect`

```kex
intersect(other: Set<A>) -> Set<A>
```

Returns the elements both sets have.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: the intersection

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).intersect(Set.from([2, 3, 4]))   # => Set(2, 3)
Set.from([1]).intersect(Set.from([2]))               # => Set()
```

_Which requested permissions the user actually has_

```kex
requested.intersect(granted)
```

#### `difference`

```kex
difference(other: Set<A>) -> Set<A>
```

Returns the elements of this set that `other` does not have.

`a.difference(b)` and `b.difference(a)` differ. `symmetricDifference` gives the elements in either one.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the set to subtract

**Returns**: the elements only this set has

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).difference(Set.from([2]))   # => Set(1, 3)
```

_Which required fields are still missing_

```kex
required.difference(Set.from(form.keys))
```

#### `symmetricDifference`

```kex
symmetricDifference(other: Set<A>) -> Set<A>
```

Returns the elements that are in exactly one of the two sets.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: the symmetric difference

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2]).symmetricDifference(Set.from([2, 3]))   # => Set(1, 3)
```

_What changed between two snapshots_

```kex
before.symmetricDifference(after)
```

#### `subset?`

```kex
subset?(other: Set<A>) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when every element of this set is also in `other`. The empty set is a subset of everything.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the candidate superset

**Returns**: `true` when this set is contained in `other`

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2]).subset?(Set.from([1, 2, 3]))   # => true
Set.from([1, 9]).subset?(Set.from([1, 2, 3]))   # => false
```

_An authorisation check_

```kex
required.subset?(granted)
```

#### `superset?`

```kex
superset?(other: Set<A>) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when this set has every element of `other`; the reverse of `subset?`.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the candidate subset

**Returns**: `true` when this set contains all of `other`

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).superset?(Set.from([1, 2]))   # => true
Set.from([1, 2]).superset?(Set.from([1, 9]))      # => false
```

#### `disjoint?`

```kex
disjoint?(other: Set<A>) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the two sets share no element.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: `true` when the intersection is empty

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2]).disjoint?(Set.from([3]))      # => true
Set.from([1, 2]).disjoint?(Set.from([2, 3]))   # => false
```

_Checking that two rulesets cannot both apply_

```kex
allowList.disjoint?(denyList)
```

#### `+`

```kex
+(other: Set<A>) -> Set<A>
+(other: [A]) -> Set<A>
```

Returns the union with another set or with a list.

The list form is a short way to add elements: +s + [x]+.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the elements to add

**Returns**: the union

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2]) + [3]           # => Set(1, 2, 3)
Set.from([1]) + Set.from([2])    # => Set(1, 2)
```

#### `-`

```kex
-(other: Set<A>) -> Set<A>
-(other: [A]) -> Set<A>
```

Returns this set without the elements of another set or of a list.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the elements to remove

**Returns**: the difference

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]) - [2]                # => Set(1, 3)
Set.from([1, 2, 3]) - Set.from([2, 3])   # => Set(1)
```

#### `map` (from Enumerable)

```kex
map(f: (A -> B)) -> Set<B>
```

Applies `f` to every element and returns a set of the results.

If `f` sends two elements to the same value, the result has it once, so the result can be smaller than the set.

**Parameters**

  - `f` — applied to each element

**Returns**: the distinct results

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).map { |x| x * 2 }   # => Set(2, 4, 6)
Set.from([1, -1]).map { |x| x.abs }     # => Set(1)
```

_Collecting the distinct extensions in a file list_

```kex
Set.from(paths).map { |p| p.split(".").last.or("") }
```

#### `filter` (from Enumerable)

```kex
filter(pred: (A -> Bool)) -> Set<A>
```

Returns a new set with only the elements `pred` accepts.

**Parameters**

  - `pred` — the test applied to each element

**Returns**: the matching elements

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).filter { |x| x > 1 }   # => Set(2, 3)
```

#### `reject`

```kex
reject(pred: (A -> Bool)) -> Set<A>
```

Returns a new set without the elements `pred` accepts.

**Parameters**

  - `pred` — the test applied to each element

**Returns**: the elements that failed the predicate

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([1, 2, 3]).reject { |x| x > 1 }   # => Set(1)
```

#### `showValue` (from Showable)

```kex
showValue -> String
```

Renders the set as `Set(...)`, with the elements in order.

**Returns**: the rendered set

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([2, 1]).showValue   # => "Set(1, 2)"
```

#### `blank?` (from Blankable)

```kex
blank? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the set has no elements, as `empty?` does. This makes a set `Blankable`, so code that tests strings with `blank?` can test sets.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty set

**Examples**

```kex
Set.empty.blank?         # => true
Set.from([1]).blank?     # => false
```

### From [`Enumerable`](../enumerable.md#trait-enumerable)

  - [`mapIndexed`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-mapindexed) — Applies `f` to each item and its 0-based position, and returns the results as a list.
  - [`into`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-into) — Applies `f`, which returns a list, to each item and concatenates the results.
  - [`collect`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-collect) — Applies `f`, which returns an `Optional`, to each item and returns the present values, unwrapped.

### From [`Foldable`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable)

  - [`each`](../enumerable.md#foldable-each) — Calls `f` with each item, for its side effects.
  - [`eachIndexed`](../enumerable.md#foldable-eachindexed) — Calls `f` with each item and its 0-based position, for its side effects.
  - [`all?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-all?) — Returns `true` when every item satisfies `pred`, and `true` for an empty collection.
  - [`any?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-any?) — Returns `true` when at least one item satisfies `pred`, and `false` for an empty collection.
  - [`none?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-none?) — Returns `true` when no item satisfies `pred`, the opposite of `any?`.
  - [`one?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-one?) — Returns `true` when exactly one item satisfies `pred`.
  - [`find`](../enumerable.md#foldable-find) — Returns the first item satisfying `pred`, or `None` when nothing does.

### From [`Monoid`](../algebra.md#trait-monoid)

  - [`repeat`](../algebra.md#monoid-repeat) — Combines this value with itself `n` times.

### From [`Showable`](../kex.md#trait-showable)

  - [`to`](../kex.md#showable-to) — 

## record `UnorderedSet<A>`

A set stored as a map from each element to `true`.

Build one with `UnorderedSet.from`. Iteration follows the map's internal order, so use `items.sort` when you need a stable order.

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([3, 1, 2]).contains?(2)   # => true
```

**Fields**

  - `slots` : {A: [Bool](../truthyable.md#make-bool)} (optional)

Implements [`Enumerable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-enumerable), [`Foldable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable), [`Monoid`](../algebra.md#trait-monoid), [`Showable`](../kex.md#trait-showable), [`Blankable`](../blankable.md#trait-blankable).

### Functions

#### `reduce` (from Enumerable, Foldable)

```kex
reduce(acc: B, f: (B -> A -> B)) -> B
```

Folds over the elements in unspecified order.

Use a `Set` when the order of the fold matters.

**Parameters**

  - `acc` — the initial accumulator
  - `f` — combines the accumulator with each element

**Returns**: the final accumulator

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).reduce(0) { |sum, x| sum + x }   # => 6
```

#### `identity` (from Monoid)

```kex
identity -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns the empty unordered set, the `Monoid` identity for union.

**Returns**: the empty set

#### `combine` (from Monoid)

```kex
combine(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns the union of the two sets. This is the `Monoid` operation.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the set to combine with

**Returns**: every element of either set

#### `contains?`

```kex
contains?(value: A) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when `value` is a member.

This is a map lookup.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to look for

**Returns**: `true` when it is present

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).contains?(2)   # => true
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).contains?(9)   # => false
```

#### `count` (from Foldable)

```kex
count -> Integer
```

Returns the number of distinct elements.

**Returns**: the number of elements

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 1, 2]).count   # => 2
```

#### `empty?`

```kex
empty? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the set has no elements.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty set

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.empty.empty?   # => true
```

#### `items`

```kex
items -> [A]
```

Returns the elements as a list, in unspecified order.

Sort the result when you need a stable order, as in a test.

**Returns**: the elements

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([3, 1, 2]).items.sort   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

#### `add`

```kex
add(value: A) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns a new set with `value` added. Adding an existing member changes nothing.

Use `add!` to rebind the receiver variable.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to add

**Returns**: a set including `value`

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1]).add(2).count   # => 2
UnorderedSet.from([1]).add(1).count   # => 1
```

#### `delete`

```kex
delete(value: A) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns a new set without `value`. Removing a non-member changes nothing.

Use `delete!` to rebind the receiver variable.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to remove

**Returns**: a set without `value`

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2]).delete(1).count   # => 1
```

#### `union`

```kex
union(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns every element of either set.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: the union

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2]).union(UnorderedSet.from([2, 3])).count   # => 3
```

#### `intersect`

```kex
intersect(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns the elements both sets have.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: the intersection

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).intersect(UnorderedSet.from([2, 3, 4])).items.sort
# => [2, 3]
```

#### `difference`

```kex
difference(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns the elements of this set that `other` does not have.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the set to subtract

**Returns**: the elements only this set has

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).difference(UnorderedSet.from([2])).items.sort
# => [1, 3]
```

#### `symmetricDifference`

```kex
symmetricDifference(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns the elements in exactly one of the two sets.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: the symmetric difference

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2]).symmetricDifference(UnorderedSet.from([2, 3])).items.sort
# => [1, 3]
```

#### `subset?`

```kex
subset?(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when every element of this set is also in `other`.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the candidate superset

**Returns**: `true` when this set is contained in `other`

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2]).subset?(UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]))   # => true
```

#### `superset?`

```kex
superset?(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when this set has every element of `other`.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the candidate subset

**Returns**: `true` when this set contains all of `other`

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).superset?(UnorderedSet.from([1, 2]))   # => true
```

#### `disjoint?`

```kex
disjoint?(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the two sets share no element.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the other set

**Returns**: `true` when the intersection is empty

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2]).disjoint?(UnorderedSet.from([3]))   # => true
```

#### `+`

```kex
+(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> UnorderedSet<A>
+(other: [A]) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns the union with another unordered set or with a list.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the elements to add

**Returns**: the union

**Examples**

```kex
(UnorderedSet.from([1, 2]) + [3]).count   # => 3
```

#### `-`

```kex
-(other: UnorderedSet<A>) -> UnorderedSet<A>
-(other: [A]) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns this set without the elements of another unordered set or of a list.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the elements to remove

**Returns**: the difference

**Examples**

```kex
(UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]) - [2]).count   # => 2
```

#### `map` (from Enumerable)

```kex
map(f: (A -> B)) -> UnorderedSet<B>
```

Applies `f` to every element and returns an unordered set of the results. Elements that map to the same value collapse into one.

**Parameters**

  - `f` — applied to each element

**Returns**: the distinct results

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).map { |x| x * 2 }.items.sort   # => [2, 4, 6]
```

#### `filter` (from Enumerable)

```kex
filter(pred: (A -> Bool)) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns a new unordered set with only the elements `pred` accepts.

**Parameters**

  - `pred` — the test applied to each element

**Returns**: the matching elements

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).filter { |x| x > 1 }.items.sort   # => [2, 3]
```

#### `reject`

```kex
reject(pred: (A -> Bool)) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns a new unordered set without the elements `pred` accepts.

**Parameters**

  - `pred` — the test applied to each element

**Returns**: the elements that failed the predicate

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([1, 2, 3]).reject { |x| x > 1 }.items   # => [1]
```

#### `showValue` (from Showable)

```kex
showValue -> String
```

Renders the set as `UnorderedSet(...)`.

The elements are printed sorted, so the same set always prints the same.

**Returns**: the rendered set

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([2, 1]).showValue    # => "UnorderedSet(1, 2)"
UnorderedSet.from([10, 2]).showValue   # => "UnorderedSet(2, 10)"
```

#### `blank?` (from Blankable)

```kex
blank? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the set has no elements, as `empty?` does.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty set

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.empty.blank?   # => true
```

  - [`mapIndexed`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-mapindexed) — Applies `f` to each item and its 0-based position, and returns the results as a list.
  - [`into`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-into) — Applies `f`, which returns a list, to each item and concatenates the results.
  - [`collect`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-collect) — Applies `f`, which returns an `Optional`, to each item and returns the present values, unwrapped.

### From [`Foldable`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable)

  - [`eachIndexed`](../enumerable.md#foldable-eachindexed) — Calls `f` with each item and its 0-based position, for its side effects.
  - [`all?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-all?) — Returns `true` when every item satisfies `pred`, and `true` for an empty collection.
  - [`any?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-any?) — Returns `true` when at least one item satisfies `pred`, and `false` for an empty collection.
  - [`none?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-none?) — Returns `true` when no item satisfies `pred`, the opposite of `any?`.
  - [`one?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-one?) — Returns `true` when exactly one item satisfies `pred`.

## module `Data.Set`

Constructors for the sorted `Set`.

### `from`

```kex
from(items: [A]) -> Set<A>
```

Builds a sorted set from a list, discarding duplicates.

**Parameters**

  - `items` — the elements, in any order and with any duplicates

**Returns**: the distinct elements, sorted

**Examples**

```kex
Set.from([3, 1, 2, 3])    # => Set(1, 2, 3)
Set.from("hello".chars)   # => Set(e, h, l, o)
```

_Removing duplicates from a list_

```kex
Set.from(["b", "a", "b"]).items   # => ["a", "b"]
```

### `empty` (constant)

```kex
empty : Set<A>
```

Returns the empty set, the `Monoid` identity: `s.combine(Set.empty)` is `s`.

**Examples**

```kex
Set.empty.empty?   # => true
Set.empty.add(1)   # => Set(1)
```



## module `Data.UnorderedSet`

Constructors for the hash-backed `UnorderedSet`.

### `from`

```kex
from(items: [A]) -> UnorderedSet<A>
```

Builds an unordered set from a list, discarding duplicates.

Unlike `Set.from`, this does not need the elements to be `Comparable`.

**Parameters**

  - `items` — the elements, in any order and with any duplicates

**Returns**: the distinct elements

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.from([3, 1, 2, 3]).count   # => 3
```

_A fast membership test over a large list_

```kex
let stopWords = UnorderedSet.from(["the", "a", "of"])
words.reject { |w| stopWords.contains?(w) }
```

### `empty` (constant)

```kex
empty : UnorderedSet<A>
```

Returns the empty unordered set, the `Monoid` identity.

**Examples**

```kex
UnorderedSet.empty.empty?   # => true
```

  - { kind: module, name: "Data" }

# Data.Stack

## module `Data`

A last-in-first-out stack.

Nothing here is in scope until `using Data.Stack`.

```kex
using Data.Stack
```

`push`, `pop` and `peek` take constant time. `items` lists the elements bottom to top, the order they were pushed in:

```kex
let s = Stack.from([1, 2, 3])
s.peek                                         # => Just(3)
s.push(4).items                                # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
s.pop.map { |top, rest| (top, rest.items) }    # => Just((3, [1, 2]))
Stack.empty.pop                                # => None
```

Every update returns a new stack. `push!` rebinds the variable to the result, as `add!` does for `Data.Set`.



## record `Stack<A>`

A stack of elements.

Build one with `Stack.from`. The record literal takes its elements top first, the reverse of `items`.

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

**Fields**

  - `elements` : [A] (optional)

Implements [`Enumerable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-enumerable), [`Foldable<A>`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable), [`Monoid`](../algebra.md#trait-monoid), [`Showable`](../kex.md#trait-showable), [`Blankable`](../blankable.md#trait-blankable).

### Functions

#### `reduce` (from Enumerable, Foldable)

```kex
reduce(acc: B, f: (B -> A -> B)) -> B
```

Folds the elements from bottom to top, the order of `items`. `map`, `each` and the other `Enumerable` functions use the same order.

**Parameters**

  - `acc` — the initial accumulator
  - `f` — combines the accumulator with each element

**Returns**: the final accumulator

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).reduce(0) { |sum, x| sum + x }   # => 6
```

#### `identity` (from Monoid)

```kex
identity -> Stack<A>
```

Returns the empty stack, the `Monoid` identity.

**Returns**: the empty stack

#### `combine` (from Monoid)

```kex
combine(other: Stack<A>) -> Stack<A>
```

Pushes the elements of `other` onto this stack, bottom first, so the top of `other` ends up on top.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the stack to push on top

**Returns**: this stack with `other` stacked above it

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2]).combine(Stack.from([3, 4])).items   # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
```

#### `items`

```kex
items -> [A]
```

Returns the elements bottom to top, the order they were pushed in.

**Returns**: the elements, bottom first

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

#### `push`

```kex
push(value: A) -> Stack<A>
```

Returns a new stack with `value` pushed on top.

`s.push!(value)` rebinds `s` to the result.

**Parameters**

  - `value` — the element to push

**Returns**: a stack with `value` on top

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2]).push(3).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

#### `pop`

```kex
pop -> (A, Stack<A>)?
```

Returns the top element and the stack without it, or `None` for an empty stack.

**Returns**: the top element and the rest, or `None`

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).pop.map { |top, rest| (top, rest.items) }
# => Just((3, [1, 2]))
Stack.empty.pop   # => None
```

#### `peek`

```kex
peek -> A?
```

Returns the top element, or `None` for an empty stack.

**Returns**: the top element, or `None`

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).peek   # => Just(3)
Stack.empty.peek             # => None
```

#### `count` (from Foldable)

```kex
count -> Integer
```

Returns the number of elements.

**Returns**: the number of elements

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).count   # => 3
```

#### `empty?`

```kex
empty? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the stack has no elements.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty stack

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.empty.empty?         # => true
Stack.from([1]).empty?     # => false
```

#### `+`

```kex
+(other: Stack<A>) -> Stack<A>
+(other: [A]) -> Stack<A>
```

Pushes the elements of another stack or of a list onto this one.

A list is read bottom to top, as by `Stack.from`, so its last element ends up on top.

**Parameters**

  - `other` — the elements to push

**Returns**: this stack with `other` pushed above it

**Examples**

```kex
(Stack.from([1, 2]) + [3, 4]).items            # => [1, 2, 3, 4]
(Stack.from([1, 2]) + Stack.from([3])).items   # => [1, 2, 3]
```

#### `showValue` (from Showable)

```kex
showValue -> String
```

Writes the stack as `Stack(...)`, bottom to top.

**Returns**: the rendered stack

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).showValue   # => "Stack(1, 2, 3)"
```

#### `blank?` (from Blankable)

```kex
blank? -> Bool
```

Returns `true` when the stack has no elements, like `empty?`.

**Returns**: `true` for the empty stack

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.empty.blank?         # => true
Stack.from([1]).blank?     # => false
```

### From [`Enumerable`](../enumerable.md#trait-enumerable)

  - [`map`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-map) — Applies `f` to each item and returns the results as a list.
  - [`mapIndexed`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-mapindexed) — Applies `f` to each item and its 0-based position, and returns the results as a list.
  - [`filter`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-filter) — Returns the items for which `pred` returns `true`.
  - [`into`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-into) — Applies `f`, which returns a list, to each item and concatenates the results.
  - [`collect`](../enumerable.md#enumerable-collect) — Applies `f`, which returns an `Optional`, to each item and returns the present values, unwrapped.

### From [`Foldable`](../enumerable.md#trait-foldable)

  - [`each`](../enumerable.md#foldable-each) — Calls `f` with each item, for its side effects.
  - [`eachIndexed`](../enumerable.md#foldable-eachindexed) — Calls `f` with each item and its 0-based position, for its side effects.
  - [`all?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-all?) — Returns `true` when every item satisfies `pred`, and `true` for an empty collection.
  - [`any?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-any?) — Returns `true` when at least one item satisfies `pred`, and `false` for an empty collection.
  - [`none?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-none?) — Returns `true` when no item satisfies `pred`, the opposite of `any?`.
  - [`one?`](../enumerable.md#foldable-one?) — Returns `true` when exactly one item satisfies `pred`.
  - [`find`](../enumerable.md#foldable-find) — Returns the first item satisfying `pred`, or `None` when nothing does.

### From [`Monoid`](../algebra.md#trait-monoid)

  - [`repeat`](../algebra.md#monoid-repeat) — Combines this value with itself `n` times.

### From [`Showable`](../kex.md#trait-showable)

  - [`to`](../kex.md#showable-to) — 

## module `Data.Stack`

Constructors for `Stack`.

### `from`

```kex
from(items: [A]) -> Stack<A>
```

Builds a stack from a list read bottom to top, so the last element is on top.

**Parameters**

  - `items` — the elements, bottom first

**Returns**: the stack, with `items`'s last element on top

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.from([1, 2, 3]).peek   # => Just(3)
```

### `empty` (constant)

```kex
empty : Stack<A>
```

Returns an empty stack.

**Examples**

```kex
Stack.empty.empty?   # => true
```

---
package: prelude
version: "0.4.0-rc.5-dev"
source: kex/ast.kex
title: Kex.AST
entities:
  - { kind: module, name: "Kex.AST" }
